225.title: Come to me for refuge
225.hook: after seventeen chapters on duty, Krishna says: come to me for refuge, and do not grieve
225.carry: take refuge in god, and do not grieve
225.howItsDone: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, Gita 18.66 is honored as the charama shloka, the final verse, and is central to the teaching of surrender (prapatti); teachers in other traditions also give it a central place.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yathecchasi: reflect fully, then do as you choose, and you are deeply loved. Your line was God teaches, then trusts you to choose. Today, the verse that comes right after.

A child learning to swim. For weeks: kick like this, cup your hands like that, turn your head, breathe. Rules and more rules. Then one day the parent stands in the water, arms open, and says: forget all that. Just come to me. I've got you. The rules weren't wrong. But there's a moment when trust does what technique can't. In one Hindu tradition, the verse right after Krishna hands the choice back is that moment. They call it the charama shloka, the final verse.
screen: `KICK, CUP, TURN, BREATHE.` → `THEN: FORGET ALL THAT.` → `COME TO ME. I'VE GOT YOU.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty-six. Abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all wrongs. Do not grieve. Sarva-dharman parityajya, mam ekam sharanam vraja. Commentators have argued over every word. What does abandon all dharmas mean, after a whole book about doing your dharma? The Sri Vaishnava tradition, which follows Ramanuja, calls this the charama shloka and reads it as surrender, prapatti: stop relying on your own efforts to save yourself, and rely on God's grace alone. Shankara reads it as renouncing all actions and taking refuge in the one self. Other teachers read dharmas here as your anxieties about merit and demerit, not your duties: keep acting, but let go of the scorekeeping. However the first line is read, the verse ends with two words: ma shuchah. Do not grieve. The Gita began with Arjuna grieving, and it ends with Krishna telling him not to. Verses sixty-seven to seventy-one are about passing the teaching on. Don't tell it to someone who doesn't want to hear it. Whoever shares it with those who love it is most dear. Even someone who only listens with faith, without scoffing, finds freedom. Then verse seventy-two. After all that, Krishna asks: have you heard this with a focused mind, Arjuna? Is your confusion gone? The teacher checks in. For devotional Hindus this is the heart of bhakti: in the end you aren't saved by getting every rule right. You lean on God. That's the last instruction: take refuge, don't grieve, and did you hear me?
screen: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS, COME TO ME.` · `THREE READINGS, ONE VERSE.` · `DO NOT GRIEVE.` · `HAVE YOU HEARD THIS, ARJUNA?` · then, large: `ABANDON ALL DHARMAS.`

segments.voice: In a hard moment, many Hindus simply say a name of God and lean on it. Notice what you're carrying today: the rules, the scores, the trying to get it all right. If you pray, say quietly, sharanam, refuge, or a name of God that's yours. If you don't, just set the weight down for a few breaths. Then hear the last two words: do not grieve.
Sharanam, refuge, shelter. Gita eighteen, sixty-six: abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all wrongs; do not grieve.
Your line: take refuge in God, and do not grieve. A book that began in grief ends with ma shuchah. See you tomorrow.

226.title: Where victory lives
226.hook: the Gita ends with its narrator telling a blind king where victory really lies
226.carry: god's grace and your effort, together
226.howItsDone: When Hindus recite the whole Gita, the reading closes with Sanjaya's words in 18.74–18.78; the last verse, on fortune and victory wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, is sometimes recited on its own as a blessing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sharanam: abandon all dharmas, come to me alone. Your line was take refuge in God, and do not grieve. And Krishna asked: is your confusion gone? Today, Arjuna answers, and the book ends.

Go back to the very first verse. An old blind king, Dhritarashtra, sits in his palace far from the battlefield. His sons lead one army. His nephews, Arjuna and his brothers, lead the other. He can't see, so he asks his charioteer Sanjaya, who has been given the gift of seeing far off: what are they doing? The entire Gita, every word, has been Sanjaya's answer. The king was hoping for news of his sons. What he got was this. Today, Sanjaya speaks for the last time.
screen: `A BLIND KING IN HIS PALACE.` → `WHAT ARE THEY DOING?` → `THE WHOLE GITA IS THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: First, Arjuna. Verse seventy-three: my confusion is gone. I've found my memory again, through your grace. I stand firm, my doubts are gone. I will do what you say. Karishye vachanam tava. In chapter one he was shaking. Now he stands. Then Sanjaya. Verse seventy-four: I have heard this wondrous conversation between Krishna and the great-souled Arjuna, and my hair stands on end. Verse seventy-five: by the grace of Vyasa, the sage the Mahabharata names as its author, I heard this highest secret, this yoga, from Krishna, the lord of yoga himself, speaking it directly. Verse seventy-six: remembering again and again this wondrous and holy dialogue, I rejoice, again and again. Verse seventy-seven: remembering that astonishing form of Hari, great is my wonder. Then verse seventy-eight, the last verse of the Gita. Wherever there is Krishna, the lord of yoga, wherever there is Arjuna, the archer, there is fortune, victory, well-being and sound judgment. That is my conviction. It's quietly pointed: Sanjaya is telling a king who wanted his own sons to win exactly where victory lies. Krishna, the lord of yoga, holds the reins. Arjuna, bow in hand, does the fighting. Many teachers read the verse as grace and effort together: not grace without effort, not effort without grace, but both in one chariot. It's why many Hindus begin their work with a prayer, then put their whole effort in. The war still has to be fought; the Mahabharata goes on.

segments.voice: Do what Sanjaya does: remember. Let one moment from these weeks of the Gita come back to you: the lamp in a windless place, the upside-down tree, your own dharma. Then think of one thing you'll work at tomorrow. If you pray, offer it before you start, as many Hindus do. If you don't, picture doing your full part, and leaving room for what you can't control.

227.title: Action, devotion, knowledge
227.hook: Arjuna's whole journey from collapse to standing, and the three roads to God it teaches
227.carry: three roads to god: action, devotion, knowledge
227.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often speak of three yogas, or paths: karma (action), bhakti (devotion) and jnana (knowledge); some read the Gita's eighteen chapters as three sets of six built around them, and some Hindus recite the whole Gita on Gita Jayanti.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sanjaya's closing: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is victory. Your line was God's grace and your effort, together. That was the last verse. Today, the whole road from the first one.

Go back to the first morning. Two armies face each other on the field of Kurukshetra. Conches blow. Arjuna asks Krishna, his charioteer, to drive between the lines so he can see who he's about to fight. He sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His mouth goes dry. I won't fight, he says, and he drops his bow and sits down in the chariot. That's chapter one. Seven hundred verses later, the same man stands up. Today, how he got there, in one go.
screen: `TWO ARMIES. ONE CHARIOT.` → `HE DROPS HIS BOW.` → `SEVEN HUNDRED VERSES LATER, HE STANDS.`

segments.voice: Krishna doesn't answer with one argument. He answers with three roads, and Hindus have walked all three ever since. One traditional teaching aid splits the eighteen chapters into three sets of six to show them. The first road is karma yoga, the yoga of action. Chapters one to six: do your work, offer it, and let go of the fruit. You have a right to the action, not to its result. The second road is bhakti yoga, the yoga of devotion. Chapters seven to twelve: love God. Offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, Krishna says, and I accept it. The third road is jnana yoga, the yoga of knowledge. Chapters thirteen to eighteen: know what you really are. The body is a field, and the one who knows the field is your true self; one light shines in every field. The labels are a teaching aid; all three run through the book. And in chapter eighteen they meet: reflect fully, then choose; come to me for refuge. Arjuna says, my confusion is gone, and stands. Here's the big Hindu idea under it: there isn't only one way up. Someone who serves, someone who sings to God, someone who asks hard questions: each is on a real road, and most people walk some of all three. That's why one Hindu home can hold a grandmother at her altar, a father who calls his work his offering, and a teenager who won't stop asking why.

Devotion: if you pray, say a name of God you love; if you don't, think of someone you love without asking anything back. Knowledge: ask quietly, who is the one noticing all this? Notice which road felt most like home.

228.title: Grief becomes a verse
228.hook: Valmiki's grief at a hunter's arrow becomes the first shloka, and why Hindus carry verses by heart
228.carry: sacred verses are carried by heart
228.howItsDone: Many Hindus learn a few verses by heart, often from parents or grandparents, and recite them at puja and in hard moments; the Vedas were handed down orally for centuries, and children still learn Gita verses and whole chapters by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gita: one conversation, three roads. Your line was three roads to God: action, devotion, knowledge. Today, where a verse comes from, and where it lives.

A sage named Valmiki goes down to a river to bathe. On a branch nearby, two krauncha birds, a mated pair, are calling to each other. A hunter's arrow strikes one, and it falls; its mate cries out over it. Valmiki is overwhelmed, and words burst out of him, a curse on the hunter. But the words come out in an even rhythm, four lines of eight syllables, as if they'd been made to be sung. He walks back stunned by what he's said.
screen: `TWO BIRDS ON A BRANCH.` → `AN ARROW.` → `GRIEF COMES OUT IN RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: The Ramayana tells what happens next. Valmiki realizes his grief, shoka, has come out as verse, and he calls it shloka. Then Brahma, the creator, visits him and tells him to use this meter to tell the story of Rama. That's how, the tradition says, the Ramayana began: grief turned into verse. Valmiki is honored as the adi kavi, the first poet. The shloka became the meter of the great epics, and much of the Gita is in it too. Notice what it's built for: short lines with a beat, made to be chanted and remembered. For most of Hindu history, scripture lived less on the page than in the voice. The Vedas were passed down by memory, teacher to student, for centuries. In Hindi, a verse you know by heart is kanthastha: resting in the throat. That's today's teaching. In Hinduism, sacred words aren't only read. They're carried inside you, in sound, and said when they're needed: at a puja, before an exam, at a bedside. So here are a few candidates from these weeks. Two, forty-seven: your right is to the action, not its fruit. Six, five: lift yourself by yourself. Nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, some water, offered with love. Eighteen, sixty-six: come to me for refuge; do not grieve. Keep one that stayed with you, or any other. There's no correct list. Your own, even if imperfect, is better, as the Gita says of your own dharma.
screen: `SHOKA BECOMES SHLOKA.` · `VALMIKI, THE FIRST POET.` · `KANTHASTHA: HELD IN THE THROAT.` · `FOUR VERSES TO CHOOSE FROM.` · then, large: `KEEP ONE BY HEART.`

segments.voice: Choose your verse, just one. Say it softly, in Sanskrit if you know it, or in your own words. Say it again, slower, and notice where it sits: the throat, the chest. Say it a third time on the out-breath. That's how Hindu families have handed verses down for generations: not by reading, by saying, again and again.
Shloka, a verse. Born, the Ramayana says, from Valmiki's shoka, his grief; made to be held in the throat.

229.title: Even Arjuna forgot
229.hook: after the war, Arjuna admits he's forgotten the Gita, and why Hindus study scripture every day
229.carry: svadhyaya: study the sacred words daily
229.howItsDone: Many Hindus read or recite the Gita regularly: a few verses each morning, a chapter a day across eighteen days, or a full recitation on Gita Jayanti in the month of Margashirsha; svadhyaya, one's own study of sacred texts, is counted as a spiritual discipline.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shloka: Valmiki's grief became the first verse. Your line was sacred verses are carried by heart. Today, what happens when they aren't.

The war is over. The Pandavas have won, at a terrible cost, and Yudhishthira rules as king. One day Arjuna and Krishna are spending time together in the palace, and Arjuna admits something astonishing. Remember what you taught me before the battle? I've forgotten it. Tell me again. The man who heard the Gita from Krishna himself, on the field, has lost it.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `REMEMBER WHAT YOU TAUGHT ME?` → `I'VE FORGOTTEN IT.`

segments.voice: This is in the Mahabharata, in a book after the war, the Ashvamedhika Parva. Krishna isn't pleased. He says he taught it in a state of yoga, and he can't simply say it all again the same way. So he teaches him again, in other words, a teaching called the Anugita, the song after. Teachers draw a plain lesson from it: hearing once, even from God, isn't enough. That's why Hinduism has svadhyaya. Sva, your own; adhyaya, study, recitation. Your own regular study of sacred words. The Gita names it among the divine qualities, and in its discipline of speech. The Taittiriya Upanishad's teacher tells the student who is leaving: don't neglect your study. The yoga tradition counts it among its core observances. So Hindus keep rhythms for it. Some read a chapter a day, finishing the Gita in eighteen days, then start again. Some read a few verses each morning. Many temples and homes celebrate Gita Jayanti, the Gita's birthday, in the month of Margashirsha, often with a full recitation. And the same verse says different things in a different year; the Gita itself keeps returning to letting go of the fruit, in chapter two, three, five and eighteen. Svadhyaya isn't homework you finish. It's how the words stay alive in you, so a line turns up uninvited, halfway through a hard phone call.
screen: `KRISHNA TEACHES IT AGAIN.` · `SVADHYAYA: YOUR OWN STUDY.` · `DON'T NEGLECT YOUR STUDY.` · `A VERSE A DAY, A CHAPTER A DAY.` · then, large: `STUDY IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Take your verse from yesterday. If you pray, say it once before a picture of God or a lamp, the way many Hindus begin the day. If you don't, just say it once, slowly. Then picture tomorrow, waking, the hardest hour, the drive home, and place the verse somewhere in that day, like a note in a coat pocket. Arjuna forgot; you're leaving yourself a way back.
Svadhyaya, one's own study: reading and reciting the sacred words again and again, because even Arjuna forgot.
Your line: svadhyaya: study the sacred words daily. Even Arjuna needed to hear it twice. Until tomorrow.

230.title: The battle inside
230.hook: how a book set on a battlefield became Gandhi's guide to nonviolence, and Tilak's call to act
230.carry: anasakti: act fully, don't cling to the fruit
230.howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of nishkama karma, action without craving for the result, and try to work this way, often offering the work to God; Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga and Tilak's Gita Rahasya are still widely read in India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, svadhyaya: even Arjuna forgot, and had to hear it again. Your line was svadhyaya: study the sacred words daily. Today, two men who studied it for years and came out with opposite answers.

London, the late eighteen-eighties. A young law student from Gujarat meets two brothers who ask him to read the Gita with them. He's embarrassed: he's never read it, not in Sanskrit, not in Gujarati. So he meets it first in English, in Edwin Arnold's poem The Song Celestial. His name is Mohandas Gandhi. Years later, in South Africa, he copies verses onto slips of paper and learns them by heart while he gets ready each morning, and the Gita becomes, as he put it, his dictionary of daily reference.
screen: `A LAW STUDENT IN LONDON.` → `AN ENGLISH POEM.` → `VERSES ON SLIPS OF PAPER.`

segments.voice: But the Gita is set on a battlefield, and Krishna is telling Arjuna to fight. How does a man of nonviolence live by it? Gandhi read the battle as the war inside every person, between what's better and worse in us. And he took from the Gita one teaching above all: act fully, and let go of the fruit. In nineteen twenty-nine he finished a Gujarati translation and called it Anasakti Yoga, the yoga of non-attachment. Hindus also call this nishkama karma, action without craving: do what's right completely, without clinging to how it turns out. It's chapter two, verse forty-seven: your right is to the action, not its fruit. Now Bal Gangadhar Tilak. Jailed by the British in Mandalay, in Burma, he wrote a long Marathi commentary, the Gita Rahasya, published in nineteen fifteen. His reading: the Gita's heart is karma yoga, energetic action in the world, and duty can include resisting wrong by force. Same book, same verse about the fruit, and the two men disagreed sharply. That argument is still alive. But what both men kept is the teaching itself. Work for what's right with everything you have, and don't let the result own you. A student before an exam, a volunteer in the temple kitchen, someone fighting for a cause that may not win in their lifetime: do the work, offer the fruit.
screen: `THE BATTLE INSIDE.` · `ANASAKTI: NON-ATTACHMENT.` · `TILAK: ACTION, FROM A JAIL CELL.` · `SAME VERSE, OPPOSITE READINGS.` · then, large: `ACT FULLY. DON'T CLING.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're working toward that you can't fully control: a grade, a game, someone's answer. If you pray, offer it, as many Hindus do: the work is mine, the fruit is yours. If you don't, say to yourself: I'll do my part fully, and let the result go. Then picture tomorrow's piece of it, done wholeheartedly, with open hands.

231.title: The walk home
231.hook: the old rite that ended a student's years with the teacher, and its last words: treat the guest as God
231.carry: speak truth, live dharma, honor the guest as god
231.tomorrow: The Isha Upanishad: all this is pervaded by the Lord
231.howItsDone: In traditional Hindu education, the end of study was marked by samavartana, the student's ceremonial return home; the teacher's final advice in Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 is still recited at some convocations in India, and 'atithi devo bhava', the guest is as God, is still taught to children and lived at many Hindu tables.

segments.voice: Yesterday, anasakti: Gandhi's Gita, the battle inside. Your line was act fully, don't cling to the fruit. Today, the last day of this long stretch with the Gita.

In ancient India, a student lived for years in the teacher's house, learning the Vedas by heart, tending the fire, fetching water. When the studies were done, there was a rite called samavartana: the return home. The student bathed, put on new clothes, and the teacher gave a last talk. One version of that talk survives in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Then the student walked home, carrying it all. Today is your samavartana.
screen: `YEARS IN THE TEACHER'S HOUSE.` → `A BATH, NEW CLOTHES.` → `THEN, THE WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: The teacher's talk is still one of the best-known passages in Hinduism. Satyam vada: speak the truth. Dharmam chara: live by dharma. Don't neglect your study, the svadhyaya from two days ago. And then four short lines many Indian children still learn: matri devo bhava, pitri devo bhava, acharya devo bhava, atithi devo bhava. Let your mother be as God to you. Your father. Your teacher. And your guest. That last one is why, in so many Hindu homes, a guest is fed first and fed too much: the guest at the door is treated as the divine come to visit. Notice where the teaching sends the student. Not to a cave. Home: to parents, to guests, to a household. In Hindu thought, the student's years are one stage of life, and they open into the householder's life of dharma, lived at home. That's where these weeks with the Gita lead too. A man who drops his bow, and the same man standing up. Refuge, and do not grieve. Victory where God and the human act together. Three roads. Verses carried by heart, and studied again. Act fully, and let go of the fruit. Plenty of people keep a Gita on a shelf and never read it through; you walked it, one piece at a time. Tomorrow the path goes deeper, into the Upanishads, the texts the Gita draws on, starting with the Isha: all this is pervaded by the Lord. But today, like the student, take the bath, put on the new clothes, and walk home with it.
screen: `SATYAM VADA. DHARMAM CHARA.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST AS GOD.` · `NOT TO A CAVE. HOME.` · `LOOKING BACK AT THE GITA.` · then, large: `THE WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: Picture the student's last morning: the bath, the new clothes, the teacher's last words. Now think of the home you'll walk into today. Choose one of the teacher's lines for it: speak the truth, or treat the next person at your door as you'd treat God. If you pray, ask for help keeping it; if not, just hold the intention. Then walk home with your one Gita verse.
